prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a new way of measuring, which is the criterion I weigh most. Katori's magic-wavelength idea cancels the trapping light shift, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once and fractional uncertainties reach the 1e-18 level. The result has been independently reproduced at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree at that level. That agreement is the experimental evidence I look for, rather than a single laboratory claiming a record. The clocks already deliver measurements that were out of reach, such as gravitational redshift over millimetres, tests of the constancy of constants and relativistic geodesy, and they drive the discussion of redefining the second. The two-name credit is clean: Katori for the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the technique to the lowest systematic uncertainty and to many-body regimes. Opening support is also broadest here (four rankings, three first places), and I do not treat that as merit in itself, but nothing in the colleagues' openings has undermined the scientific case.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness. Ye's frequency-comb work was part of the 2005 prize context and ion clocks were recognised in 2012, so a sceptical member can call lattice clocks an extension of already honoured precision-metrology rather than a separate discovery. There is also a timing point: the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and one could argue the prize should wait for that. Finally, a two-name credit leaves out strong contributors such as Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Derevianko and Takamoto, and the prize would be tilted toward the experimental accuracy race over the earlier proposal work of others. I think the first two points are weaker than they look, since the magic-wavelength scheme is a new physical idea and the redefinition depends on, not defines, the achievement, but I cannot dismiss them.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first as a simple physical trick (the magic wavelength) that opens a precision regime, sees the two-person credit as clean, and asks whether the committee treats clocks as a continuation of the comb prize or as a separate discovery.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the pairing, and I would answer her question directly: the comb prize gave a ruler for optical frequencies, while the lattice clock is a different object, a many-atom oscillator whose systematic shifts are engineered away. The difference is the same as between a good ruler and a calibrated instrument that uses it. I would add one caution to her use of 'a continuation': if the committee frames it as a continuation, the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly so the prize does not look like a second award for combs. I also share her note that Ye's appearance in a molecule candidate is only a credit-overlap question, not a scientific one.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first for the detector-driven discovery of high-energy neutrinos, with Halzen as a clean single credit, and ranks the BeppoSAX gamma-ray burst afterglow work second; he ranks the lattice clocks third and says he is outside atomic physics.
responses.response: I take the detector-driven argument seriously, because I weigh instruments heavily too, and the diffuse flux is very well confirmed. My reservation on B021 is attribution rather than science: a cubic-kilometre detector is built by a large collaboration and by AMANDA and DUMAND before it, and a single name is a stronger statement than the record supports from the supplied material. For the clocks the credit problem is much smaller, and the maturity is demonstrated by many laboratories reaching the same 1e-18 level independently. On B007 I would press the point he himself raises: one of the key optical-afterglow people is deceased and the supplied names leave out other decisive observers, so I find that configuration harder to defend than the clocks. I recognise he may weigh timeliness differently, since an unrealised redefinition of the second could be read as either a reason to wait or to recognise now.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a general mechanism with broad reach across solids, photonics and cold atoms, and notes that the allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the uncredited Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a real problem.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I do not dismiss it; the experimental confirmation is extensive and independent, and recognition is arguably overdue. Where I differ is that the attribution problem he describes is not a footnote: any three of the four credited names omits Mele or Hasan, and the supplied list omits the HgTe theory proposers whose prediction Molenkamp's experiment tested, so a fair prize might need more than the three-person limit allows. I also note the 2016 prize on topological phases is a context he does not weigh and I would not call it a barrier. That is why I keep B024 as my first alternative, but would rather give the prize where the credit is unambiguous. I accept that breadth of reach is a valid criterion and that clocks are narrower in the communities they touch.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first because nature gave the clue and the result opened a new window on the cosmos, and he leaves Halzen as a clean single credit while flagging uncertainty about the collaboration and earlier pioneers; he does not rank lattice clocks in the shortlist positions.
responses.response: I accept that the diffuse neutrino flux is robust and that opening a new window is the kind of result the prize is meant for. I disagree that being nature-driven should count for more than being instrument-driven: the lattice clock is also an observation of nature, since it measures redshift and tests constancy of constants to a precision that decides questions. On his own flagged uncertainty about a single laureate, I share it, and I would add that his list of AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers is a reason to expect a contested citation. If the committee wants an astro-particle prize I would want the attribution question resolved before I support it over the clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, or as an extension of them.
I recall but have not verified the latest fractional-uncertainty figures and the status of the second-redefinition roadmap, so timing is a judgement from memory.
Whether a prize limited to Katori and Ye is fair to Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke and other contributors, and whether the citation should name the lattice scheme or the clock broadly.
If the committee prefers a topological or sensing prize, whether B024 can be configured without leaving out a decisive contributor, and whether B027 is one discovery or three.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connection, not obviously disqualifying: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is at JILA, where Hall worked, so I know that environment, although I have no joint work or supervision relationship with Ye or Katori on the provided profile. Separately, my background in precision laser spectroscopy and quantum optics means I am close to this field, so colleagues should weigh my view with that in mind. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
